note:
v1, EXTREME AND MEAN: THE SEVENTH SONG, A SKELETON (Harry, 17 Nov about 03:40: "open up 2 new song slots"). The record's slow song: 80, where the other six run 100 to 138.
The riff is two cells, a long (three sixteenths) and a short (two), and one rule: every long becomes a long and a short, every short becomes a long. Apply it again and again and you get a pattern of longs and shorts that never falls into a loop, yet every stretch of it comes back, and it is the same at every size. So the band plays the one pattern at many sizes at once: the guitars' muted strokes are the smallest cells; where a cell of eight or five sixteenths begins the string is let ring; where one of thirteen or eight begins there is a chord; where one of thirty-four or twenty-one begins, a crash; and the song's own eight sections go long, short, long, long, short, long, short, long: the long ones heavy, the short ones quiet. The form is the riff, 78 times slower. The kit keeps common time against all of it and starts its count again with each section.
In the quiet sections a wire harp (new on this record) has no written notes: the engine is given the same rule and plays it, each short cell a step higher than the long one that made it. In the last section the harp plays over the band.
The title is Euclid's phrase for a line cut so that the whole is to the longer part as the longer is to the shorter. Such a cut has no common measure; neither has this riff.
WHERE THINGS ARE: heavy 0:00, quiet 0:44, heavy 1:11, heavy on A flat with four guitars 1:54, quiet 2:38, heavy 3:05, quiet 3:49, heavy with the harp 4:16, one chord 4:59.

WHAT I MEASURED (I cannot listen): compscore 99.89 / 99.93 (seeds 0 and 11). That is not a verdict on a skeleton: the scorer rewards the 5 to 7 dB between the heavy and the quiet sections.
- The quiet sections sit 4.9, 6.1 and 6.6 dB under the heavy ones before them; the four-guitar sections are 1 dB over the two-guitar ones.
- Against the records the five heavy stretches are within 2.3 dB in every band. The two-guitar ones are 1.5 to 2.3 dB short between 500 Hz and 4 kHz.
- In the quiet sections the harp leads (2.6 dB under the whole), the bass is 2.6 under it, the clean guitar's chords and the soft kick about 3 under it again. Over the band the harp sits level with the quieter guitars.
- My first levels were wrong, as usual: the harp was 12 dB too loud in the quiet sections (they were louder than the heavy ones) and 13 dB over the whole band in the last one.
- It is slow, not sparse: the scorer counts 6.0 onsets a second, as on the other six.
WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether at 80 it reads as heavy or only as slow; whether a riff that never repeats reads as a riff or as stumbling; whether the harp sounds like a harp or like a cheap pluck; whether three quiet sections on the same nine bars (one a minor third up, one an octave up) are a breath or a wait.
A CARD (one): "A slow song at 80: heavy, or only slow?"
NOT HEARD BY ANYONE.
SWITCH: the third field of C10T7_HARP set to nothing takes the harp out of the last section.
next: Harry's ear on the card (heavy or only slow; the harp). Then, by the draw: the quiet sections are the same nine bars three times (a second voice, or the rule read another way); a lead for the four-guitar sections; the two-guitar sections' mids; the unused colours the brief lists (freeze, chamber, brush) where the song has a reason.
